readings.title: Dating an old street photograph
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An archive received a photograph of a market street. The donated note gave a year, but a shop sign appeared to belong to a later period. The main obstacle was a date based on unverified memory. A family had kept the image for decades without recording when it was taken. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used comparison with dated maps and advertisements. Archivists checked businesses visible in the image against independent records. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated the photograph was probably several years newer. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a catalogue date marked as an estimate. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: archives should distinguish evidence from memory. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in dating an old street photograph, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Recording memories of a factory
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Former workers shared memories of a closed factory. Interviews were valuable, yet several accounts disagreed about the year one workshop opened. The main obstacle was oral accounts treated as identical timelines. People remembered the same change from different jobs and life stages. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used interviews compared with employment records. Researchers invited participants to review transcripts and checked available dated documents. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated the differences revealed distinct viewpoints. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced notes that show both confirmed dates and memories. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: historical disagreement can be informative. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in recording memories of a factory, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Opening a map collection online
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A museum digitised old town maps. Visitors searched by present street names and failed to find maps labelled with earlier names. The main obstacle was catalogue terms that changed over time. The original descriptions reflected the date of each map but not modern search habits. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a sample of unsuccessful searches. Cataloguers compared current and historical place names without altering the images. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated alternative names improved discovery. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced search tags that link old and current names. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: digital access depends on thoughtful description. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in opening a map collection online, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A school visit to the archive
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A class visited an archive to study local migration. Students enjoyed seeing letters but struggled to read the old handwriting. The main obstacle was source material without accessible entry points. The visit assumed that pupils could immediately understand unfamiliar scripts and references. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a trial worksheet using short excerpts. Teachers and archivists noted which details students recognised and which needed explanation. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated small guided examples opened deeper questions. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced transcriptions beside selected original letters. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: historical sources need context without hiding originals. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a school visit to the archive, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for local history and archives must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the local history archive programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于地方历史与档案的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the archive education team about a community activity related to local history and archives. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the local history archive programme. People have noticed a date based on unverified memory, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
